items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: The transcript mentions 'Snake Hips' in a narrative description of an incident involving 'Connie' and waiters, but the interviewee does not claim a personal relationship, meeting, or collaboration with Snake Hips.

ctx.x: Connie was a reasonable fellow but did not stand for his show people to be abused. And the waiters were tough also so no client could get away with whatever they thought they could with the entertainers or the orchestra when their drinks got too heavy for them to carry.

When Snake Hips hit the one who had thrown the hot piece, the others - three men - jumped up to defend their friend. But some of the waiters were already standing at their table, so they dug and froze. Connie came up and ordered them to pay their bill and get the hell out of there before he took a poke at one of them.

I never cared for gangsters the same as many other people, but one night one of America's biggest gangsters came to Connie's and I talked with him. He was Dutch Shultz. items.q: 'Snake-Hips' Tucker was a tough guy and loved to fight. When he did his number the customers would throw dollar bills on the floor just to see him do a summersault and go into a split to pick them up.

ctx.x: section consisted of Glyn Pague and Henry 'Moon' Jones on altos, Bingie Madison tenor. Jimmy Arckey was still there on trombone and Lee Blaire played guitar.

'Snake-Hips' Tucker was a tough guy and loved to fight. When he did his number the customers would throw dollar bills on the floor just to see him do a summersault and go into a split to pick them up. One night a table of college guys were with some girls and one of these fellows heated a half-dollar and threw it on the floor.
